stem: A train leaves a station in Bulawayo. It accelerates uniformly from rest to $18\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ in $45\ \text{s}$, travels at $18\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ for $120\ \text{s}$, and then decelerates uniformly to rest at the next station in $30\ \text{s}$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Define acceleration.

points.description: Rate of change of velocity (change in velocity per unit time)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the acceleration during the first $45\ \text{s}$, in $\text{m s}^{-2}$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the distance between the two stations, in m.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the average speed for the journey, in $\text{m s}^{-1}$.
parts.explanation: $2835/195 = 14.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. ($9\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, the mean of 0 and 18, ignores the long constant-speed stage.)
parts.workedSolution: 1. $2835/195 = 14.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. ($9\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, the mean of 0 and 18, ignores the long constant-speed stage.)

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Calculate the magnitude of the deceleration, in $\text{m s}^{-2}$.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: In practice the deceleration is not uniform: it is small at first and increases as the train nears the platform. Describe how the final section of the velocity-time graph would differ from a straight line, and state how the distance travelled while braking could still be found.

points.description: The graph curves: shallow gradient at first, becoming steeper (gradient = deceleration increasing) as it reaches zero
The distance is still the area under the (curved) graph, found by counting squares or splitting into strips

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The final section would be a curve that starts with a small negative gradient and becomes steeper until it meets the time axis, because the gradient is the acceleration. The braking distance is still the area under the curve, found by counting squares or dividing it into narrow strips.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: For the first 45 s, which graph would be a straight line through the origin?

options.content: distance travelled against (time)²
options.rationale: Correct: from rest s = ½at², so s ∝ t².

options.content: distance travelled against time
options.rationale: s is proportional to t², so this graph curves upwards.

options.content: velocity against (time)²
options.rationale: v = at is proportional to t, not t².

options.content: acceleration against time
options.rationale: The acceleration is constant: a horizontal line, not through the origin.

parts.explanation: From rest with uniform acceleration $s = \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$: $s$ against $t^2$ is a straight line through the origin of gradient $a/2$.

explanation: Gradients give the accelerations (0.40 and $-0.60\ \text{m s}^{-2}$); the area gives 2835 m, an average speed of $14.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.
hints: Acceleration = gradient; distance = area under the v-t graph.
Average speed = total distance ÷ total time.

stem: A ball is thrown from the edge of a flat roof $22\ \text{m}$ above level ground with a velocity of $15\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ at $30^\circ$ above the horizontal. Air resistance is negligible; $g = 9.81\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: State why the horizontal component of the ball's velocity remains constant.

points.description: No horizontal force acts (weight is vertical, air resistance negligible), so there is no horizontal acceleration

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The only force on the ball is its weight, which is vertical, so there is no horizontal force and no horizontal acceleration.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the initial

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: horizontal component of velocity, in $\text{m s}^{-1}$;

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: vertical component of velocity, in $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the maximum height of the ball above the ground, in m.
parts.explanation: Rise above the roof: $\dfrac{7.5^2}{2 \times 9.81} = 2.87\ \text{m}$; height above ground $= 22 + 2.87 = 24.9\ \text{m}$.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Rise above the roof: $\dfrac{7.5^2}{2 \times 9.81} = 2.87\ \text{m}$; height above ground $= 22 + 2.87 = 24.9\ \text{m}$.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the time from release until the ball hits the ground, in s.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Calculate the horizontal distance from the building to where the ball lands, in m.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Suggest how air resistance would change the maximum height and the horizontal distance, and explain why.

points.description: Both are smaller: the maximum height is lower and the ball lands closer to the building
Air resistance opposes the velocity, so it reduces the vertical component on the way up and the horizontal component throughout

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The maximum height and the horizontal distance would both be smaller. Air resistance acts against the velocity, so on the way up it adds to the downward force, slowing the rise, and it continuously reduces the horizontal velocity, so the ball lands closer to the building.

explanation: Components 13.0 and 7.5 m s⁻¹; maximum height 24.9 m; flight time 3.02 s; range 39.2 m.
hints: The ground is 22 m below the launch point: s = −22 m.

stem: A $6.0\ \text{kg}$ box rests on a smooth ramp inclined at $30^\circ$ to the horizontal. A light string parallel to the ramp passes over a smooth pulley at the top and supports a hanging $4.0\ \text{kg}$ mass. The system is released from rest; the hanging mass falls and the box moves up the ramp. Take $g = 9.81\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which force is the Newton's third-law partner of the pull of the string on the box?

options.content: the component of the box's weight down the ramp
options.rationale: This acts on the box itself and is gravitational, not a contact force from the string.

options.content: the weight of the hanging mass
options.rationale: This acts on the hanging mass and is gravitational.

options.content: the normal contact force of the ramp on the box
options.rationale: This acts on the box and is perpendicular to the ramp.

options.content: the pull of the box on the string
options.rationale: Correct: same type, equal and opposite, on the other body.

parts.explanation: Third-law partners act on different bodies and are of the same type: string on box ↔ box on string.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the component of the box's weight acting down the ramp, in N.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the acceleration of the system, in $\text{m s}^{-2}$.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the tension in the string, in N.
parts.explanation: Hanging mass: $mg - T = ma$, so $T = 4.0(9.81 - 0.981) = 35.3\ \text{N}$. Check with the box: $T - 29.4 = 6.0 \times 0.981$.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Hanging mass: $mg - T = ma$, so $T = 4.0(9.81 - 0.981) = 35.3\ \text{N}$. Check with the box: $T - 29.4 = 6.0 \times 0.981$.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Explain why the tension in the string is less than the weight of the hanging mass.

points.description: The hanging mass accelerates downwards, so the resultant force on it must be downwards
So its weight must be greater than the upward tension (T = m(g − a))

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The hanging mass accelerates downwards, so by Newton's second law the resultant force on it is downwards. The upward tension must therefore be smaller than its weight: T = m(g − a).

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Calculate the speed of the box after it has moved $0.80\ \text{m}$ up the ramp from rest, in $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

explanation: Resolve the box's weight along the ramp (29.4 N); the system's acceleration is $0.981\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ and the tension 35.3 N.
hints: Treat the box and hanging mass as one system for the acceleration.
Only the component of the box's weight along the ramp opposes the motion.

stem: On a level, frictionless track, trolley A ($0.60\ \text{kg}$) moves to the right at $0.90\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ and trolley B ($0.25\ \text{kg}$) moves to the left at $0.50\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. They collide head-on and are in contact for $0.040\ \text{s}$. Afterwards A moves to the right at $0.12\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: State the principle of conservation of momentum.

points.description: The total momentum of a system remains constant
provided no resultant external force acts on it

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The total momentum of a system of interacting bodies is constant, provided no resultant external force acts on the system.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the velocity of B after the collision, in $\text{m s}^{-1}$ (positive to the right).
parts.explanation: Right positive: $0.60(0.90) + 0.25(-0.50) = 0.60(0.12) + 0.25v_B$, so $0.415 = 0.072 + 0.25v_B$ and $v_B = 1.37\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ (to the right). Ignoring B's initial direction gives 2.37.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Right positive: $0.60(0.90) + 0.25(-0.50) = 0.60(0.12) + 0.25v_B$, so $0.415 = 0.072 + 0.25v_B$ and $v_B = 1.37\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ (to the right). Ignoring B's initial direction gives 2.37.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the total kinetic energy transferred to other forms in the collision, in J.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: What type of collision is this?

options.content: elastic, because momentum was conserved
options.rationale: Momentum is conserved in every collision of a closed system; elastic means kinetic energy is conserved too.

options.content: inelastic, because the total kinetic energy decreased
options.rationale: Correct: kinetic energy is not conserved.

options.content: elastic, because the trolleys did not stick together
options.rationale: Not sticking does not make a collision elastic.

options.content: perfectly inelastic, because the trolleys moved off together
options.rationale: They moved off with different velocities.

parts.explanation: The kinetic energy fell, so the collision is inelastic (but not perfectly inelastic, as the trolleys separate).

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Calculate the average force exerted on B during the collision, in N.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: State the magnitude and direction of the average force exerted on A during the collision.

points.description: 11.7 N to the left (equal and opposite, Newton's third law)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: 11.7 N to the left: by Newton's third law the force of B on A is equal and opposite to the force of A on B.

explanation: Momentum gives $v_B = 1.37\ \text{m s}^{-1}$; 0.0346 J of kinetic energy is transferred (inelastic); the force on B is 11.7 N, equal and opposite to that on A.
hints: Give B's initial velocity a negative sign.
Force = change of momentum ÷ contact time.

stem: Thandeka determines the density of a metal cylinder. Her readings: diameter $d = 2.54 \pm 0.01\ \text{cm}$, length $l = 4.00 \pm 0.01\ \text{cm}$, mass $m = 172.6 \pm 0.1\ \text{g}$. The volume of a cylinder is $\tfrac{1}{4}\pi d^2 l$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: State the SI base units of density.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Which instrument is most suitable for measuring the diameter of the cylinder to ±0.01 cm?

options.content: a metre rule
options.rationale: Its resolution, 0.1 cm, is ten times too coarse.

options.content: a micrometer screw gauge with a 0–25 mm range
options.rationale: Its range ends at 25 mm, just below the 25.4 mm diameter.

options.content: vernier calipers
options.rationale: Correct: resolution 0.1 mm = 0.01 cm, and the jaws fit around a 2.5 cm cylinder.

options.content: a protractor
options.rationale: A protractor measures angles.

parts.explanation: Vernier calipers read to 0.1 mm (0.01 cm) and have the range needed.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the density of the metal, in $\text{kg m}^{-3}$, to three significant figures.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the density, to two significant figures.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Calculate the absolute uncertainty in the density, in $\text{kg m}^{-3}$, to one significant figure.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: The calipers read 0.03 cm when closed and Thandeka did not correct for this. State the type of error and its effect on her value of the density.

points.description: A systematic (zero) error: every diameter reading is 0.03 cm too large
So the volume is too large and the calculated density is too small

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: It is a systematic error (a zero error): every diameter is 0.03 cm too large, so the calculated volume is too large and her density is too small.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: Suggest why she should measure the diameter at several places and in different directions.

points.description: The cylinder may not be perfectly circular or uniform, so a mean of several readings is more representative

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The cylinder may be slightly oval or tapered, so the mean of several readings gives a more representative diameter.

explanation: $\rho = 8520\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$ with 1.1 % uncertainty (the squared diameter dominates), i.e. $(8.52 \pm 0.09) \times 10^{3}\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$.
hints: Convert g cm⁻³ to kg m⁻³ by multiplying by 1000.
d is squared: double its percentage uncertainty.

stem: A small plastic sphere of mass $0.012\ \text{kg}$ is dropped from a tall building. The air resistance on it is $D = kv^2$, where $k = 2.5 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{kg m}^{-1}$ and $v$ is its speed. Take $g = 9.81\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Define terminal velocity.

points.description: The constant (maximum) velocity reached when the resistive force(s) balance the weight (driving force), so the resultant force is zero

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The constant velocity reached when the drag on a falling object equals its weight, so the resultant force and acceleration are zero.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the weight of the sphere, in N.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the acceleration of the sphere when its speed is $12\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, in $\text{m s}^{-2}$.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the terminal velocity of the sphere, in $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Explain why the acceleration of the sphere decreases from its initial value to zero.

points.description: At release the speed is zero, so there is no drag: acceleration = g
As the speed increases the drag increases, so the resultant force (weight − drag) decreases and the acceleration decreases
When drag equals weight the resultant force is zero, so the acceleration is zero (terminal velocity)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: At release the sphere is at rest, so there is no drag and its acceleration is g. As it speeds up, the drag increases, so the resultant downward force (weight minus drag) and hence the acceleration decrease. When the drag equals the weight the resultant force is zero and the acceleration is zero: the sphere falls at terminal velocity.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Which describes the velocity-time graph of the sphere?

options.content: A straight line of gradient g up to the terminal velocity, then horizontal.
options.rationale: The acceleration decreases gradually, not suddenly.

options.content: A curve from the origin with initial gradient g, levelling off at the terminal velocity.
options.rationale: Correct: the gradient (acceleration) falls from g to zero.

options.content: A curve that becomes steeper and steeper.
options.rationale: The acceleration decreases, so the gradient decreases.

options.content: A horizontal line at the terminal velocity.
options.rationale: The sphere starts from rest.

parts.explanation: The v-t graph starts with gradient g and curves over to a horizontal line at the terminal velocity.

explanation: Weight 0.118 N; at $12\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, $a = 6.81\ \text{m s}^{-2}$; terminal velocity $21.7\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ when $kv^2 = mg$.
